materials.text:
Slide 2 — The Problem: Attorneys spend 40–60% of billable hours on lower-order tasks: drafting routine contracts, reviewing discovery documents, synthesizing case law, and preparing deposition outlines. At $500–$1,200 per hour, that is a structurally expensive bottleneck baked into a $300B U.S. legal market and a $1.5T global one.

Slide 4 — The Market: U.S. legal services market is $300B annually. Global legal spend exceeds $1.5 trillion. Enterprise in-house counsel and AmLaw 100 firms represent $85B of that. No purpose-built LLM product exists for this segment today. Existing tools — Westlaw, LexisNexis, Relativity — are research databases and document repositories, not workflow AI. We are not competing with them; we are automating the work that sits on top of them.

Slide 6 — The Product: Harvey is a generative AI assistant trained on legal corpora and integrated directly into attorney workflows. Current capabilities: (1) Contract drafting and redlining across M&A, employment, real estate, and commercial agreements; (2) Due diligence review — extract, classify, and flag provisions across hundreds of documents in minutes; (3) Legal research synthesis — Harvey reads primary sources and drafts a memo-style summary with citations; (4) Deposition and hearing preparation — generates question outlines, flags prior testimony inconsistencies. Harvey operates as a co-pilot. Attorneys review, edit, and sign off before any work product is submitted.

Slide 8 — Differentiation: We are not a wrapper around a general-purpose model. Harvey is fine-tuned on over one billion tokens of legal text — case law, regulatory filings, transaction documents, and model agreements. The model has materially lower hallucination rates on legal tasks than GPT-4 in our internal benchmarks. We pair retrieval-augmented generation with the LLM so answers are grounded in the documents the attorney actually uploads, not just parametric memory. No competitor — LexisNexis AI, Clio, Ironclad — operates at this level of legal domain specificity for BigLaw and enterprise in-house.

Slide 10 — Traction: Three AmLaw 50 pilot customers signed. Total committed ARR from pilots: $1.24M. Average contract value: $413K. All three pilots are expanding seat counts. We have not churned a single customer. Pilot-to-paid conversion rate: 100%.

Slide 12 — Go-to-Market: Land in one practice group, expand firm-wide. Firms buy by practice area (M&A, litigation, real estate). Upsell path is horizontal — every attorney in the firm is a potential seat. Partner-driven sales; our first three customers came through partner introductions at Sequoia and OpenAI Startup Fund. We are intentionally not doing outbound yet.

Slide 14 — Team: Winston Weinberg (CEO) — former Goldman Sachs and Sullivan & Cromwell attorney; practiced M&A for seven years. Gabriel Pereyra (CTO) — former research scientist at DeepMind and Google Brain; led projects on large-scale language model training. Team of 14. Six engineers, four lawyers, two GTM, two operations.

Slide 16 — The Ask: Raising $21M Series A. Use of proceeds: 60% engineering (model training, infra, security), 25% GTM (first sales hire, 3 pilot expansions to full-firm), 15% G&A. 18-month runway to Series B with $4M+ ARR milestone.

materials.name: Founder Call Transcript.txt
materials.text:
Investor: Walk me through the customer situation in detail.

Winston: Sure. We have three firms — all AmLaw 50. I can't name them on this call yet but one is a Magic Circle firm with a U.S. presence, one is a top-five U.S. litigation shop, and one is a large in-house legal team at a Fortune 100. They came in as paid pilots at $400K ACV each. The Magic Circle firm started with eight seats in M&A. They expanded to 22 seats within six weeks. The litigation shop started in discovery review — they used Harvey to process 140,000 documents in a matter in about three days. A full associate team would have taken three weeks. They're now expanding into brief drafting.

Investor: What does NRR look like on those three?

Winston: It's early — all three signed in the last four months — but seat expansion in that window puts us above 140% NRR on the cohort. The M&A firm went from 8 to 22 seats. The litigation firm just signed an expansion for 15 more seats starting next month. That's the pattern we expect: land small, prove ROI in one matter, expand horizontally.

Investor: Any concerns about model dependency? You're on GPT-4.

Winston: Fair challenge. We use GPT-4 as the base, and we've fine-tuned significantly on top of it. Our retrieval layer means the base model's parametric knowledge is less critical than in a general assistant — we're always grounding answers in uploaded documents. That said, we're watching model availability risk closely. We're in active conversations with Anthropic and have a provisional agreement with OpenAI that gives us some assurance, but we don't have multi-model redundancy today. That's a known gap.

Investor: Hallucination risk in a legal context seems like an existential concern. How do you handle it?

Winston: Every Harvey output is labeled as a draft. Attorneys must review before filing or sending. We don't position Harvey as autonomous — it's a co-pilot. We've also built output confidence indicators and citation links back to source documents. In our pilot benchmarks, hallucination rates on in-context tasks are under 2%. On tasks outside the uploaded corpus, the model is trained to say it doesn't know rather than invent. We're not claiming zero hallucination — no honest AI company can. But we believe our rate is materially lower than general-purpose tools for in-scope legal tasks.

Investor: What's the regulatory picture? Are bar associations going to be a problem?

Winston: The ABA has issued preliminary guidance that AI use in legal practice is permissible provided attorneys maintain supervisory responsibility. We actually lean into that — our product design assumes human review is always final. Several state bars are still deliberating, which creates some uncertainty. We expect a patchwork of guidance over the next 12–18 months. Our view is that firms using Harvey with proper review workflows will be compliant, but we're not giving legal advice about legal AI use.

Investor: Gross margin?

Winston: We're at 62% gross margin today. Compute is the main COGS driver — we're running inference on GPT-4 and storing document embeddings. As we grow, we expect to get to 70%+ with volume discounts and potentially switching some inference to our own fine-tuned models. We're not there yet.

Investor: What happens if OpenAI changes pricing or access terms?

Winston: That is our single biggest operational risk right now, and I want to be straight with you about it. We have a revenue-share arrangement with OpenAI through the Startup Fund, but the API terms are not locked for the long term. We're mitigating by building model-agnostic retrieval infrastructure so we could swap base models. But today, if OpenAI changed GPT-4 pricing materially, our unit economics would move. We're modeling that scenario.

materials.name: Website and Product Overview.txt
materials.text:
Harvey — Legal AI for the World's Leading Law Firms

Harvey is an AI platform purpose-built for legal professionals at AmLaw 100 firms and Fortune 500 in-house legal teams. It is not a chatbot. It is a workflow tool that integrates with the documents, precedents, and processes attorneys already use.

Core Capabilities:

1. Contract Drafting — Generate first drafts of NDAs, employment agreements, commercial contracts, and M&A transaction documents. Harvey references your firm's precedent library when generating. All output is a draft requiring attorney review.

2. Due Diligence — Upload data room documents and instruct Harvey to extract, classify, and flag provisions of interest (change of control, IP assignment, indemnification caps). Harvey processes hundreds of documents and delivers a structured summary in minutes.

3. Legal Research — Ask Harvey a legal question. It searches case law and secondary sources, synthesizes findings, and drafts a research memo with inline citations. Does not replace primary source verification by the attorney.

4. Deposition Preparation — Upload prior deposition transcripts and expert reports. Harvey identifies inconsistencies, organizes prior testimony by topic, and generates a suggested question outline.

Important Limitations: Harvey generates draft work product only. No Harvey output should be submitted to any court, regulator, counterparty, or client without review, editing, and approval by a licensed attorney. Harvey is not a substitute for legal judgment. Attorneys remain professionally responsible for all work product.

Security and Data Handling: All client matter data is processed in an isolated tenant environment. Documents are not used to train or retrain Harvey's models. SOC 2 Type I certification completed; Type II audit in progress. Enterprise customers may deploy in private cloud on request.

Pricing: Enterprise annual contracts. Minimum engagement $250K ARR. Seat-based pricing; discounts at 50+ seat tiers. No self-serve or SMB offering.

materials.name: Competitive and Market Analysis Notes.txt
materials.text:
Legal AI Competitive Landscape — Harvey Internal Analysis, February 2023

Market Context:
U.S. legal services market: approximately $300B annually (IBISWorld, 2022). Global legal services: $1.5T (Statista estimate). In-house corporate legal teams represent approximately 30% of total spend. AmLaw 100 firms collectively bill approximately $120B annually. The segment most relevant to Harvey — complex transactional and litigation work at large firms and Fortune 500 in-house — is roughly $85B.

Known AI legal tools and their limitations:

Westlaw Edge / Lexis+ AI (Thomson Reuters, RELX): Both companies have launched AI-assisted research features. These are effectively search augmentation — better ranking, brief summary generation, citator integration. Neither product drafts documents or processes data room materials. Target users are associates and paralegals performing research. Not a workflow product.

Clio: Practice management SaaS for solo and small-firm attorneys. Recently announced AI features for time entry and client communications. Exclusively SMB and mid-market. No BigLaw presence. Completely different ICP from Harvey.

Ironclad: Contract lifecycle management for in-house teams. AI features are extraction and workflow routing, not generative drafting. Strong product, good funding ($333M Series E, October 2021), but positioned for contract operations teams, not practicing attorneys.

Spellbook (formerly Rally): Contract drafting AI using GPT-3/4, integrated with Microsoft Word. Small team (20 employees), Series A stage, targeting SMB law firms and solo practitioners. Pricing is $100-200/month self-serve. Not BigLaw.

Harvey's assessment: No current competitor is purpose-built for complex legal tasks at AmLaw 100 or Fortune 500 scale with a model fine-tuned on legal corpora. The field is open at the enterprise end. The risk is that Thomson Reuters or a well-funded startup copies the approach within 12–18 months.

Risks and Mitigants:
- Bar association regulatory uncertainty: ABA Model Rules permit AI use with attorney supervision. Harvey's product design (draft-only, attorney-final) is structured to comply. Risk is state-level patchwork and client-specific prohibitions.
- Model dependency (OpenAI GPT-4): Base model terms not locked. Building model-agnostic retrieval layer as mitigation. Active conversations with Anthropic.
- Enterprise security concerns: SOC 2 Type I complete, Type II in progress. Private cloud option in development.
- Accuracy / hallucination: Lower rate than general models on in-scope tasks per internal testing. No third-party benchmark published yet.
- Incumbent response: Thomson Reuters announced $100M AI investment in January 2023. Microsoft announced Copilot integration with Word, which could provide competition in document drafting broadly.
